stories.title: German Police Hunted A Criminal Who Did Not Exist
stories.description: For sixteen years the same woman's DNA appeared at forty crime scenes in three countries. Europe's most wanted phantom turned out to be a flaw in the evidence itself. #UnsolvedMysteries #Forensics #BizarreHistory
stories.editorial_rationale: The brief's strongest hook examples state one impossible fact cold (Overtoun Bridge's 300 dogs, 107.3% hook hold), so this opens on one woman at forty crime scenes and saves the countries and dates for later.

factual_claims.text: Between 1993 and 2009 the same unidentified female DNA profile was recovered from about 40 crime scenes in Germany, Austria and France, six of them murders.
German police ran a dedicated task force, Parkplatz, at Heilbronn police headquarters and raised the reward to 300,000 euros in January 2009.
The profile was recovered at the scene of the killing of police officer Michele Kiesewetter in Heilbronn on 25 April 2007 as well as at minor property crimes far away.
In March 2009 investigators concluded the DNA had already been present on the cotton swabs before they were used to collect samples, so no such offender existed.

The DNA belonged to a woman working at the factory that made the swabs, and the case led the International Organization for Standardization to publish ISO 18385 in 2016 for DNA-free forensic consumables.

segments.narration: One woman's DNA turned up at forty crime scenes. She was tied to burglaries, car thefts and six killings across three countries over sixteen years.
Germany built a task force for her and raised the reward to 300,000 euros. No witness ever described her. No camera ever caught her.
Her profile sat beside a murdered police officer in Heilbronn, and beside petty break-ins hundreds of miles away. What criminal leaves DNA and nothing else?
In March 2009, investigators finally tested the swabs themselves. The DNA was already on them, before anyone touched a single crime scene.
It belonged to a woman at the factory that packed them. The hunt ended, and in 2016 the ISO published a standard for DNA-free swabs.

research.summary: From 1993 to 2009 the same unidentified female DNA profile was recovered from roughly 40 crime scenes in Germany, Austria and France, including six murders — among them the killing of police officer Michele Kiesewetter in Heilbronn on 25 April 2007. German police ran the Parkplatz task force from Heilbronn headquarters and raised the reward to 300,000 euros in January 2009, yet no witness or image of the 'Phantom of Heilbronn' ever surfaced. In March 2009 investigators established that the DNA was already present on the cotton swabs used to collect samples: the swabs came from a single factory, sterile but not certified DNA-free, and the profile belonged to a woman who worked there. No such offender existed. The case prompted ISO 18385 (2016), the standard for DNA-free forensic consumables.

factual_claims.text: The Nebra sky disc was found in 1999 by two metal detectorists working without a licence, and is a bronze disc about 30 cm across carrying gold symbols including stars.
The finders sold the hoard the day after finding it for 31,000 German marks, and it then changed hands on the black market.
The disc is dated to about 1800-1600 BCE, in the Early Bronze Age Unetice culture.
In February 2002 state archaeologist Harald Meller recovered the disc in a police-led sting in Basel, where the holders had offered it for 700,000 marks.
A cluster of seven gold dots on the disc is interpreted as the Pleiades, and the two gold arcs on its sides mark the angle between the solstice sunsets, about 82 degrees.

segments.narration: Two unlicensed treasure hunters dug up a Bronze Age sky map. A bronze plate thirty centimetres wide, studded with gold stars.
They had no permit, so they sold it the next day for thirty-one thousand marks. It disappeared into the black market and kept changing hands.
Think about what was being passed around. Something made thirty-six hundred years ago, traded by dealers who could not read a mark on it.
In 2002 a state archaeologist posed as a buyer in a Basel hotel. Police took the disc back. The sellers had wanted seven hundred thousand marks for it.
Then the scientists read it. Seven dots are the Pleiades, and the gold arcs on the rim mark exactly where the sun sets at the solstices.

research.summary: The Nebra sky disc was dug out of the Mittelberg hill near Nebra, Germany in 1999 by two unlicensed metal detectorists, Henry Westphal and Mario Renner, together with bronze swords, axes and armband fragments. They sold the hoard the next day for 31,000 DM and it circulated on the black market for two years before state archaeologist Harald Meller recovered it in a police sting in Basel in February 2002. The 30 cm, 2.2 kg bronze disc carries gold symbols read as the sun or full moon, a crescent, 32 stars including a seven-star cluster interpreted as the Pleiades, two later side arcs spanning the roughly 82 degrees between the solstice sunsets, and a bottom arc usually read as a solar boat. It is dated to about 1800-1600 BCE.

factual_claims.text: Recovery operations at Lake Toplitz in Austria brought up counterfeit British pound notes.
Lake Toplitz has no dissolved oxygen below 20 metres, its deeper water is salty, and a layer of sunken logs floats about halfway to the bottom, making deeper diving hazardous.
In 1943 and 1944 the shore of Lake Toplitz was a Nazi naval testing station where explosive charges of up to 4,000 kg were detonated at various depths.
A 1959 recovery operation brought counterfeit notes up from the lake, and diver Gerhard Zauner reported seeing a sunken aircraft below the log layer.
The forged notes came from Operation Bernhard, the SS counterfeiting programme aimed at the British economy, and later expeditions found counterfeit currency rather than gold.

segments.narration: Divers pulled crates of fake British pounds from this lake. Toplitz, in the Austrian Alps. A hundred and three metres deep, walled in by cliffs.
Nothing breathes below twenty metres down there. No oxygen, salty water, and a raft of sunken logs floating halfway to the bottom that blocks the way.
So why keep diving it? Because in 1943 the Nazis ran a naval weapons range on that shore, detonating charges of four thousand kilos.
A 1959 expedition brought up boxes of forged five-pound notes. One of the divers reported an aircraft lying somewhere below the logs.
The crates were Operation Bernhard, an SS plan to wreck Britain's economy with forgeries. Every expedition since has come back with paper. Never gold.

research.summary: Lake Toplitz in Styria, Austria is 103 metres deep, carries no dissolved oxygen below 20 metres, has salty deep water, and holds a layer of sunken logs floating roughly halfway down that makes deeper diving hazardous. In 1943-44 its shore was a Nazi naval testing station where charges of up to 4,000 kg were detonated. Crates of counterfeit Bank of England notes produced by the SS counterfeiting programme Operation Bernhard were dumped in it, and a 1959 recovery operation brought counterfeit notes up; diver Gerhard Zauner reported a sunken aircraft below the log layer. A 2000 expedition sponsored by CBS and run by Oceaneering also recovered crate remnants containing counterfeit British pounds and US dollars. No gold has ever been recovered, and reported totals for the money recovered are inconsistent between sources, so no figure is asserted here.

stories.title: Two Crews Dug Through A Mountain And Met In The Middle
stories.description: On Samos in the mid-500s BC, two teams started digging from opposite sides of a mountain and met inside it, with the floors out by only a few decimetres. Herodotus named the engineer, and the tunnel still shows how he did it. #TunnelOfEupalinos #AncientEngineering #Samos
stories.editorial_rationale: The brief's weak hook cohort (Skara Brae 52.2%, Anglo-Zanzibar 51.5%) front-loads place and date right after the opening line, so here the impossible fact leads and the surveying method is held for the turn.

hook_candidates.why: Leads on the ancient source rather than the feat itself.

factual_claims.text: The Tunnel of Eupalinos on Samos was excavated from both ends at once in the mid-6th century BC and the two headings met inside the mountain.
The tunnel is 1,036 metres long and was built to bring water from a spring on the far side of Mount Kastro into the ancient capital of Samos.
Where the two headings met, the vertical closing error was only a few decimetres.
Herodotus names the engineer as Eupalinos of Megara, son of Naustrophus, and the tunnel contains a dog-leg where the northern heading was deliberately diverted along a planned isosceles triangle.

To absorb vertical error, the northern tunnel's roof was raised 2.5 metres and the southern tunnel's floor lowered 0.6 metres, and the tunnel is regarded as the first dug from both ends using a geometry-based approach.

segments.narration: Two crews dug through a mountain and met in the middle. Samos, Greece, in the mid-500s BC. Through solid rock, by hand.
The tunnel runs one thousand and thirty-six metres. It was a water pipe, hiding a spring from anyone besieging the city.
Here is the part that should not work. Both teams were digging blind. When they met, the floors were out by less than half a metre.
Herodotus named the man responsible: Eupalinos of Megara. That odd dog-leg in the tunnel is his correction, a planned triangle swung to catch the other heading.
He also raised one roof and dropped the other floor, so a vertical miss would still meet. Greek geometry, two centuries before Euclid wrote it down.

research.summary: The Tunnel of Eupalinos runs 1,036 metres through Mount Kastro on Samos, Greece, dug in the mid-6th century BC to carry spring water into the ancient capital. It was excavated from both ends simultaneously and is described as the first tunnel dug this way using a geometry-based approach. Herodotus (Histories 3.60) records the engineer as Eupalinos of Megara, son of Naustrophus, and describes a tunnel nearly a mile long driven clean through the base of the hill. The two headings meet at a dog-leg in the middle, with a vertical closing error of only a few decimetres. Scholars reconstruct the method as geometric: a mountain line over the summit, a 20.59 m distance unit and 7.5-degree direction unit, a planned isosceles triangle with 22.5, 45 and 22.5 degree angles when the northern heading had to be diverted, a catching width widened by 17 m, and deliberate vertical slack from raising the north roof 2.5 m and lowering the south floor 0.6 m.

verification.note: Wikipedia lists both vertical adjustments and calls the tunnel the first excavated from both ends with a geometry-based approach, noting the geometry was later codified by Euclid.

stories.title: A Dead Pig Nearly Started A War In 1859
stories.description: In June 1859 an American farmer on San Juan Island shot a pig that belonged to the Hudson's Bay Company. Within two months there were 461 US soldiers with 14 cannons facing five Royal Navy warships, and the only casualty was the pig. #PigWar #SanJuanIsland #BizarreHistory

factual_claims.text: On 15 June 1859 an American settler, Lyman Cutlar, shot a pig that was eating his potatoes on San Juan Island.
The pig belonged to Charles Griffin of the Hudson's Bay Company, and both the United States and Britain claimed San Juan Island at the time.
By 10 August 1859 Colonel Silas Casey commanded 461 American soldiers with 14 cannons, opposed by five Royal Navy warships carrying 70 guns and 2,140 men.
Rear Admiral Robert L. Baynes refused to escalate, describing the dispute as a squabble about a pig.
The two sides held a joint military occupation until arbitration under the 1871 Treaty of Washington ruled for the United States on 21 October 1872, and the pig was the only casualty.

segments.narration: A pig ate a man's potatoes and nearly started a war. San Juan Island, June 1859. One shot, one dead pig, two empires.
The farmer was American. The pig worked for the Hudson's Bay Company. Both countries claimed the island, and neither government would back down an inch.
Two months later: four hundred sixty-one American soldiers and fourteen cannons against five Royal Navy warships, seventy guns, two thousand one hundred and forty men.
All of it over a pig. The British admiral flatly refused to fire, saying he would not go to war over a squabble about a pig.
So they shared the island instead, for thirteen years, until an arbitration ruling handed it to America in 1872. Total casualties: the pig.

research.summary: On 15 June 1859 Lyman Cutlar, an American settler on San Juan Island, shot a pig that was eating his potatoes. The pig belonged to Charles Griffin of the Hudson's Bay Company, and the island was claimed by both the United States and Britain. Brigadier General William S. Harney sent Captain George Pickett with 66 soldiers; by 10 August 1859 Colonel Silas Casey had 461 men and 14 cannons, facing five Royal Navy warships with 70 guns and 2,140 men under Captain Geoffrey Hornby. Governor James Douglas ordered the Americans removed, but Rear Admiral Robert L. Baynes refused to escalate 'over a squabble about a pig'. After negotiations led by Winfield Scott both sides kept a joint military occupation of about 100 men each. The 1871 Treaty of Washington set up arbitration with German Emperor Wilhelm I, who referred it to a three-man commission in Geneva; it ruled for the United States on 21 October 1872. The British withdrew on 25 November 1872 and the Americans by July 1874. There were no human casualties.

stories.title: A Rotted Ship Left A Perfect Outline In The Sand
stories.description: In 1939 a self-taught archaeologist dug into a Suffolk mound and found a 27-metre ship that no longer existed, preserved only as a shape in the sand with its iron rivets still in place. Inside was a king's treasure and no body. #SuttonHoo #AngloSaxon #Archaeology

hook_candidates.why: One concrete impossible image, and the question of what was inside stays open.

factual_claims.text: The Sutton Hoo ship burial, excavated in 1939, contained a ship about 27 metres long whose timber had decayed, leaving its shape preserved in the sand with nearly all its iron rivets in place.
The burial held a ceremonial helmet reassembled from hundreds of fragments, gold-and-garnet shoulder clasps, ten nested silver bowls, a lyre and a purse of 37 gold coins.
Each of the 37 gold coins in the purse came from a different Frankish mint.
No skeleton survived in the burial chamber, but soil analysis found phosphate traces suggesting a body once lay there, and some scholars argue the ship was a cenotaph.
Coin analysis narrows the burial to between 610 and 635, and most scholars favour Raedwald, king of the East Angles, who died around 624.

segments.narration: A rotted ship left a perfect outline in the sand. Suffolk, 1939. Twenty-seven metres of oak, gone, every iron rivet still in place.
Inside it: a war helmet in hundreds of pieces, gold and garnet shoulder clasps, ten nested silver bowls, a lyre, and a purse of thirty-seven gold coins.
Every one of those coins came from a different Frankish mint. Someone was buried here like a king. Except there was no body.
Soil tests did find phosphate, the trace a body leaves. The usual explanation is acid sand that ate the bone; some argue nobody was buried there.
The coins date the grave to between 610 and 635. Most scholars think the man in that ship was Raedwald, king of the East Angles.

research.summary: Sutton Hoo, near Woodbridge in Suffolk on the River Deben estuary, holds two Anglo-Saxon cemeteries of the 6th to 7th centuries with about 20 mounds. Landowner Edith Pretty hired the self-taught archaeologist Basil Brown in 1938; in May 1939 his team began on Mound 1 and found an iron ship rivet on the third day, and Charles Phillips then led the excavation. The ship was about 27 m long and 4.4 m wide amidships; its timber had decayed but the sand preserved its shape with nearly all the iron rivets in place. No skeleton survived, though soil phosphate traces suggest a body once lay there and some scholars have proposed a cenotaph. Finds include a reassembled ceremonial helmet, ten nested silver bowls, spoons inscribed PAULOS and SAULOS, gold-and-garnet shoulder clasps, a lyre, and a purse of 37 gold coins each from a different Frankish mint. Coin analysis narrows the burial to 610-635 and most scholars favour Raedwald of the East Angles, who died around 624.

factual_claims.text: The liner SS Waratah disappeared off the South African coast on the night of 27-28 July 1909 with 211 people aboard, on only her second voyage.

No confirmed wreckage or bodies were ever found; searches included Royal Navy cruisers and the charter ship Sabine, which covered about 14,000 nautical miles.

segments.narration: A whole liner vanished off South Africa with 211 aboard. July 1909. The Waratah, barely a year old, on only her second voyage.
She left Durban at quarter past eight in the evening. At dawn a freighter swapped lamp signals with her, then lost sight of her by mid-morning.
Nobody ever saw her again. Royal Navy cruisers searched. One chartered ship covered fourteen thousand nautical miles. Not a lifeboat. Not a body.
In 1999 sonar seemed to find her at last. Divers reached that wreck in 2001 and it was a cargo ship, sunk by a U-boat decades later.
Passengers had complained she rolled badly. The leading theory is a top-heavy ship caught by one of the twenty-metre rogue waves that coast is known for.

research.summary: SS Waratah, owned by William Lund & Sons and operated by the Blue Anchor Line on the London-Sydney route, disappeared off the South African coast on the night of 27-28 July 1909 on her second voyage, with 92 passengers and 119 crew, 211 people in total. She left Durban at 8:15 pm on 26 July, exchanged signal-lamp messages with the Clan Line freighter Clan MacIntyre at about 4 am on 27 July, and was last seen by that ship at 09:30 near the Mbashe River delta. No confirmed wreckage or bodies have ever been found. Searches included the tug Harry Escombe, the Royal Navy cruisers Pandora, Forte and Hermes, and the charter ship Sabine, which covered about 14,000 nautical miles; the line posted her missing on 15 December 1909. A wreck reported in 1999 was dived in 2001 and identified as the Nailsea Meadow, sunk by a U-boat in the Second World War. The Board of Trade inquiry could not determine a cause and attributed the loss to a storm of exceptional violence. Leading theories are instability and top-heaviness, a rogue wave (waves up to 20 m are reported off South Africa), and a shift of about 1,500 tons of lead concentrates.

factual_claims.text: Baiae, a Roman town on the Gulf of Naples, is partly submerged, with mosaics lying about 5 metres below sea level.
Seneca called Baiae a harbour of vice; Julius Caesar and Nero had villas there and Hadrian died at his villa there in AD 138.

Baiae was built around warm mineral springs, and the structure once called the Temple of Mercury is part of a thermal bath complex with a dome about 21.5 metres across, the largest in the world before the Pantheon.
The submersion of Baiae was caused by bradyseism, ground movement from volcanic activity in the Phlegraean Fields, which lowered the coastline in phases.

segments.narration: Rome's most notorious party town is now under the sea. Baiae, on the Bay of Naples. Its mosaic floors sit about five metres down.
Seneca called it a harbour of vice. Caesar kept a villa here. Nero built one. Hadrian died in his.
The whole town was built on hot mineral springs, and one bath dome was the widest in the world before the Pantheon. So what sank it?
Not a wave, not an earthquake. The ground itself. The volcanic field underneath breathes, lifting and dropping this coast by metres, and Baiae sat on the part that sank.
By the eighth century the lower town was sea floor. Since 2002 it is a protected park, and divers swim its streets past the emperors' floors.

research.summary: Baiae, on the north-west shore of the Gulf of Naples in the modern comune of Bacoli, was a fashionable Roman resort from about 80 BC with villas built from about 100 BC, notorious enough that Seneca called it a 'harbour of vice'. Julius Caesar had a villa there, Nero built one in the mid-1st century AD, Septimius Severus visited often, and Hadrian died at his villa there in AD 138. The town was built around warm mineral springs; the structure long called the Temple of Mercury is part of a thermal bath complex and its dome, about 21.5 m across, was the largest in the world before the Pantheon. Bradyseism, ground movement from volcanic activity in the Phlegraean Fields, lowered the coast in two phases, and the lower town was largely underwater by the 8th century. Mosaics and other remains lie about 5 m below sea level, with the triclinium-nymphaeum of Claudius about 7 m deep off Punta Epitaffio. An underwater archaeological park was established in 2002, and new mosaics were reported in 2023 and 2024.

factual_claims.text: Hatshepsut's cartouches and images were chiselled off or covered on her monuments and her statues were smashed or buried.
Hatshepsut ruled Egypt as pharaoh for about twenty-one years in the 15th century BC and was depicted with pharaonic regalia including the false beard.
Hatshepsut's mortuary temple stands at Deir el-Bahari and she erected twin obelisks at the entrance to the Karnak temple, one of which still stands and is the second-tallest ancient standing obelisk.
The erasure of Hatshepsut's monuments began near the end of Thutmose III's reign, decades after her death, and continued into the reign of Amenhotep II.

Historians including Joyce Tyldesley and Donald Redford explain the erasure as political, presenting the royal succession as running directly from Thutmose II to Thutmose III, rather than as personal vengeance.

segments.narration: Someone chiselled a pharaoh off her own temple walls. Hatshepsut ruled Egypt for about twenty-one years, carved in stone wearing the false beard of a king.
She left the terraced mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari and twin obelisks at Karnak. One of those obelisks is still standing today.
Then her name starts vanishing. Cartouches hacked out. Statues smashed and buried. Images plastered over. Why erase the most successful reign in a century?
Not revenge. The attacks begin near the end of her stepson's long reign, decades after her death, when any personal grudge had had a lifetime to cool.
Historians read it as paperwork. Make the crown pass straight from father to son, and the woman who reigned in between simply stops having existed.

research.summary: Hatshepsut reigned c. 1479-1458 BC, first as regent for her stepson Thutmose III and then as pharaoh in her own right from about Year 7 of his reign, for a total given by Manetho and Josephus as about 21 years 9 months. She was the second confirmed woman to rule Egypt in her own right, and was depicted with the traditional attributes of kingship including the false beard, shendyt kilt and khat headcloth with uraeus. Her mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari is considered an architectural masterpiece and she raised twin obelisks at the entrance to Karnak, one of which still stands and is the second-tallest ancient standing obelisk. Near the end of Thutmose III's reign and into Amenhotep II's, her cartouches and images were chiselled off or covered and her statues smashed or buried. Historians including Joyce Tyldesley and Donald Redford read this as political necessity, presenting succession as running directly from Thutmose II to Thutmose III, rather than personal hatred. Howard Carter found tomb KV60 in 1903; in 2007 Zahi Hawass concluded that mummy KV60A was very likely Hatshepsut, an identification a 2011 re-examination of the matching tooth cast doubt on.

stories.title: Russian Peat Held A Carved Face For 12,000 Years
stories.description: Workers pulled a nine-foot wooden idol out of a Ural peat bog in 1890, in ten pieces. In 2021 radiocarbon dating made it the oldest known wooden sculpture on Earth — twice the age of the pyramids. #UnsolvedMysteries #Archaeology #BizarreHistory
stories.editorial_rationale: The brief's best-holding hook (Mirage of Constanz, 187.7% hook hold) states a flat physical impossibility before any context, so this opens on wood surviving 12,000 years and holds the date and place back to the second sentence.

hook_candidates.why: Leads on the impossible physical fact — wood that did not rot — with a hard number attached.

factual_claims.text: The Shigir Idol was recovered from the Shigir peat bog on the eastern slope of the Middle Urals in 1890, in ten separate pieces.
The idol is carved from larch wood, stands 2.8 m (about nine feet) as reconstructed, and carries multiple carved faces plus geometric ornament; the tree was at least 159 years old when felled.
The Shigir Idol is the oldest known wooden sculpture in the world.
The idol was made by hunter-gatherers, not by a farming or city-building society.
A 2021 study in Quaternary International by the University of Gottingen and the Russian Academy of Sciences dated the idol to roughly 12,000 years ago, far older than Stonehenge.

segments.narration: A carved wooden face survived 12,000 years in a bog. Workers hauled it out of Russian peat in 1890, in ten pieces.
Larch wood, nine feet tall, cut from a tree already 159 years old. Faces stare out of it at several heights, geometric lines running between them.
Nothing else from that era is like it. So who was carving portraits before anyone farmed, built a city, or fired a pot?
The answer is the bog. Peat sealed the larch from oxygen, so it never rotted. Hunter-gatherers made monumental art; we just never had the evidence.
In 2021, new radiocarbon dates put the carving at about 12,000 years old. Older than Stonehenge by seven thousand years.

research.summary: The Shigir Idol, found in the Shigir peat bog near Yekaterinburg on 24 January 1890 and reassembled from ten fragments, is the oldest known wooden sculpture. Carved from larch and standing 2.8 m as reconstructed (Tolmachev's 1914 reconstruction suggested 5.3 m originally), it survived because waterlogged peat kept oxygen off the wood. Successive dating pushed its age from ~9,500 years to the start of the Holocene; a 2021 Quaternary International study by Gottingen and the Russian Academy of Sciences put it at roughly 12,000 years, meaning hunter-gatherers were producing monumental art millennia before farming.

factual_claims.text: The Marree Man, a figure about 2.7 km tall, was spotted from the air in June 1998 on a plateau west of Marree in outback South Australia.
The outline is about 28 km long, with lines up to 35 m wide and 20-30 cm deep, and satellite imagery shows it appeared between late May and mid-June 1998.
Anonymous press releases referred to the figure as 'Stuart's Giant', and a plaque bearing an American flag and quoting Hedley Finlayson's 1946 book The Red Centre was found at the site.

The lines run 28 kilometres, up to 35 metres wide, a foot deep. Satellite images show the whole figure appeared in under two weeks.
Anonymous faxes steered reporters to it, calling the figure Stuart's Giant and quoting an American book. Who builds this, then hides?
Suspicion settled on Bardius Goldberg, an Alice Springs artist who worked at scale and understood GPS. Friends said he admitted it to them.
Goldberg died in 2002 without ever confirming it, and a five thousand dollar reward in 2018 produced nobody. The grader marks are still there.

research.summary: The Marree Man is a geoglyph of a hunting figure holding a woomera or boomerang, cut into a plateau at Finniss Springs about 60 km west of Marree, South Australia. A charter pilot spotted it on 26 June 1998; satellite imagery dates its creation to between 27 May and mid-June 1998. It stands about 2.7 km tall with a 28 km perimeter covering ~2.5 km2, lines up to 35 m wide and 20-30 cm deep. Anonymous press releases called it 'Stuart's Giant' and a plaque with a US flag quoting Finlayson's The Red Centre was found nearby. Alice Springs artist Bardius Goldberg, who died in 2002, is the leading suspect; no creator was ever confirmed, and a A$5,000 reward in 2018 produced nothing. It was restored with GPS-guided graders in August 2016 with the Arabana Aboriginal Corporation's permission.

stories.title: France Sent An Army After One Animal In 1765
stories.description: For three years an animal hunted a single corner of south-central France, and the king sent soldiers, bloodhounds and his own hunter to stop it. The man who ended it was a local, and the answer was never a monster. #UnsolvedMysteries #BizarreHistory #France

factual_claims.text: Estimates of the Beast of Gevaudan's death toll run from about 60 to 113 people over roughly three years.
The attacks ran from 30 June 1764 to 19 June 1767 over an area of roughly 90 by 80 km in the Margeride Mountains of the former province of Gevaudan, and a 1987 study counted 210 attacks.

Louis XV sent a force under Captain Duhamel, then the professional wolf hunters Jean-Charles d'Enneval and his son with eight bloodhounds, then his hunter Francois Antoine, who reached Le Malzieu on 22 June 1765.
Antoine killed a large grey wolf, the Loup de Chazes, on 20-21 September 1765 - about 1.7 m long and 60 kg - and received over 9,000 livres, but attacks resumed afterwards.
Jean Chastel shot the animal on 19 June 1767 on Mont Mouchet, and most modern scholars attribute the deaths to one or more wolves, with public hysteria spreading belief in a single monster.

segments.narration: One animal killed over sixty people in three years. It hunted a single corner of France and would not stop.
The attacks began in Gevaudan in summer 1764 and ran for three years, across ninety kilometres of mountains. Reports counted over two hundred attacks.
Louis XV sent soldiers, then professional wolf hunters with eight bloodhounds, then his own hunter Francois Antoine. How does one animal beat all of them?
Antoine shot a huge grey wolf in September 1765, sixty kilos and nearly two metres long, and was paid nine thousand livres. The attacks started again.
A local hunter, Jean Chastel, killed the last one in June 1767. Historians now think it was never one monster, just wolves, and a province that had stopped sleeping.

research.summary: Between 30 June 1764 and 19 June 1767 a series of fatal animal attacks struck the Margeride Mountains in the former French province of Gevaudan, over an area of roughly 90 by 80 km. A 1987 study counted 210 attacks, 113 deaths and 49 injuries; other sources put the deaths at 60 to 100. Louis XV intervened: a force under Captain Duhamel, then the professional wolf hunters d'Enneval and son with eight bloodhounds, then the king's hunter Francois Antoine, who shot a 60 kg grey wolf in September 1765 and was paid over 9,000 livres. Attacks resumed, and local hunter Jean Chastel shot the animal on 19 June 1767. Most modern scholars conclude the deaths were caused by one or more wolves, with public hysteria sustaining belief in a supernatural beast; the silver-bullet detail is a later literary invention.

factual_claims.text: On 15 May 1943 armed bats were accidentally released at the Carlsbad Army Airfield Auxiliary Air Base in New Mexico and set fire to the test range.

A National Defense Research Committee observer concluded that 'X-Ray is an effective weapon', and the programme was taken over by the Navy as Project X-Ray.
About $2 million had been spent when Fleet Admiral Ernest J. King cancelled the programme after learning it would probably not be combat-ready until mid-1945.

segments.narration: Escaped bats burned down an American army airfield in 1943. The bats were armed, and that part was the Army's own idea.
A Pennsylvania dentist had written to the White House a month after Pearl Harbor, proposing bats as incendiary carriers. The plan was approved.
Each casing held 1,040 Mexican free-tailed bats in twenty-six stacked trays, every bat carrying a tiny timed napalm charge. Who signs off on this?
The fire happened during a test at Carlsbad. Observers still called the weapon effective, so the Navy took it over as Project X-Ray.
Two million dollars in, Admiral Ernest King killed it: bat bombs would not be combat-ready before mid-1945. The atomic bomb got there first.

research.summary: Project X-Ray was a US attempt to carry incendiaries into Japanese cities on bats. Dental surgeon Lytle S. Adams proposed it to the White House in January 1942; the design used a 1.5 m sheet-metal carrier with 26 trays holding 1,040 Mexican free-tailed bats, each glued to a small timed napalm incendiary of Louis Fieser's design. On 15 May 1943 armed bats escaped at the Carlsbad Army Airfield Auxiliary Air Base in New Mexico, roosted under a fuel tank and burned the test range down. Observers nonetheless judged the weapon effective and the Navy took the programme over, but Fleet Admiral Ernest J. King cancelled it after about $2 million had been spent, on the grounds that it would not be combat-ready until mid-1945; the atomic bomb overtook it.

stories.description: About 170 Viking-age blades carry the same name inlaid in iron, and seventeen of them spell it wrong. The best of them are made of steel that should not have existed in Europe at the time. #UnsolvedMysteries #Vikings #BizarreHistory
stories.editorial_rationale: The brief's Skyquake hook (125.1% hold) states a plain fact then immediately denies the obvious explanation; this opens on 170 identical signatures and then pulls the brand name apart rather than describing a sword.

factual_claims.text: About 170 swords (167 catalogued) carry the inlaid inscription +VLFBERH+T.
Ulfberht swords date from the 9th to the 11th centuries and are found mostly in Fennoscandia and around the Baltic, with 44 from Norway.
About 17 known examples carry misspelled forms of the name, such as +VLEBERHIT and +VLFBERTH.
The Frankish form of the name points to a Rhineland origin, and three Ulfberht swords were found in Volga Bulgaria, then part of the Volga trade route.
One Ulfberht example appears to have been made from high-quality hypereutectoid steel possibly imported from Central Asia.

segments.narration: About 170 Viking swords carry the same inlaid name. Ulfberht, spelled out in iron letters down the middle of the blade.
They turn up across Scandinavia and the Baltic, forty-four in Norway alone, made between the ninth and eleventh centuries.
Seventeen of them spell it wrong. Was somebody copying a name they could not read, a thousand years before trademarks?
The name is Frankish, so the workshop was probably in the Rhineland. Three of the swords turned up in Volga Bulgaria, far down the Russian river trade route.
And the best blades are not local metal at all: one is high-carbon steel that may have come from Central Asia. A Frankish brand, foreign steel, seventeen bad spellers.

research.summary: Ulfberht swords are a group of about 170 Viking-age blades, 9th to 11th century, carrying the inlaid Frankish name +VLFBERH+T. Most are found in Fennoscandia and around the Baltic (44 in Norway, 17 in Sweden, 13 in Germany), though the name's form points to manufacture in the Rhineland, with Carolingian capitularia prohibiting sale of such weapons to foreigners. About 17 examples carry misspellings such as +VLEBERHIT and +VLFBERTH, which Stalsberg attributes to illiterate labour in the smithy while also raising the possibility that the signature was copied or falsified. The group spans several steel types and methods; one example appears to be high-quality hypereutectoid steel possibly imported from Central Asia, and three swords were found in Volga Bulgaria on the Volga trade route. Metallurgist Alan Williams' analysis of +VLFBERH+T blades as crucible steel, featured in NOVA's Secrets of the Viking Sword, is the best-known statement of the imported-steel case.

stories.title: An African Spear Solved Europe's Oldest Bird Riddle
stories.description: In 1822 a white stork turned up in northern Germany with a central African spear through its neck, still alive and still nesting. That one bird settled centuries of argument about where birds go in winter. #UnsolvedMysteries #BizarreHistory #Birds
stories.editorial_rationale: Radium Girls' weaker 49.3% hook hold came from an instruction-style opener, so this leads with the physical absurdity itself in the shape of the brief's best hook, Mirage of Constanz at 187.7%.

hook_candidates.text: A stork landed in Germany with a spear through it
hook_candidates.why: A living animal carrying a weapon: strange on its face, and it asks who threw it.

hook_candidates.text: Europeans once believed storks spent the winter underwater
hook_candidates.why: Leads on the old belief, which is funny but makes the video about ideas rather than an object.

factual_claims.text: A white stork was found in 1822 near Klutz in Mecklenburg, Germany, with a spear lodged through its neck.
The spear was about 75 cm long and came from central Africa, where the bird had been wintering.
Before migration was understood, naturalists held that storks and swallows hibernated underwater or changed into other animals.
Because the spear was identified as central African, the stork must have been wounded there and flown back to Germany.
The stuffed stork is kept in the zoological collection of the University of Rostock, and about 25 Pfeilstorche had been documented in Germany as of 2003.

segments.narration: A stork landed in Germany with a spear through it. The bird was alive, nesting, behaving as if nothing had happened.
Mecklenburg, 1822. The shaft ran two and a half feet long, and no hunter in Europe carried a weapon anything like it.
So where had the bird been? Every winter Europe's storks vanished. Naturalists argued they hibernated underwater, or changed into other creatures entirely.
The spear was identified as central African. That meant the stork had been speared there, survived it, and flown thousands of miles home.
One bird proved migration. It is still in Rostock's collection, stuffed, spear included, and roughly two dozen more have turned up since.

research.summary: The Rostocker Pfeilstorch is a white stork found in 1822 near Klutz, then in the Grand Duchy of Mecklenburg-Schwerin, alive with a 75 cm central African spear lodged in its neck. Until then the winter disappearance of storks and swallows was explained by underwater hibernation or transmutation into other animals, ideas promoted by zoologists of the period. The spear's central African origin showed the bird had wintered there and flown back, which is the physical evidence for long-distance migration. The stuffed specimen is held in the zoological collection of the University of Rostock; about 25 Pfeilstorche had been documented in Germany as of 2003, and later cases include a stork from Tanganyika and a honey buzzard from Finland. Audubon's account credits the examination to Heinrich Gustav Florke and places the wound in the Upper Nile region.

sources.title: What This Gruesome Stork Taught Us About Bird Migration - Audubon

verification.claim: A stork was found in Germany in 1822 with a spear through it, still alive.
verification.note: Wikipedia: the first and most famous Pfeilstorch was a white stork found in 1822 near Klutz, Mecklenburg, with a spear lodged in its neck; the whole significance of the find is that the bird flew to Germany after being wounded, so it reached Germany alive.

verification.note: Wikipedia: before migration was understood, theories held that swallows and storks turned into other birds or mice or hibernated underwater, and zoologists of the time promoted these ideas. The 'birds flew to the moon' belief appears only in popular retellings and is deliberately left out.

verification.claim: The central African spear meant the bird had been wounded there and flown back.
verification.note: Wikipedia: the spear came from central Africa, where the bird had been wintering, and the specimen showed that birds migrate long distances rather than hibernating or changing form. 'Thousands of miles' is the real distance from central Africa to the Baltic coast and is not a figure either source states numerically.
